doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Navy Chief recruits black musicians for shore duty
summary: At 22 and 1A, he jumps at the Navy offer to avoid the infantry; he was still a raw musician.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Can I ask how old you were when you got called up?

I was 22, yeah 22 years old. Let’s see around June or July, the Navy sent a Chief Musician out to our union meetings. See we used to have separate union meetings. A black union, we would meet in Oakland at the Elks building there. They had a building with a bar upstairs and there was quite a building, a very nice building. And we would hold our meetings there. Because we were a subsidiary. And we weren’t allowed access to the Local 6 musicians headquarters. But anyhow the Navy, they sent a Chief out to recruit black musicians to be stationed on the shore, given shore duty. So it was an offer you couldn’t refuse, because I was 1A. And so—
In your head, were you thinking it’s this or perhaps the infantry?

Oh yeah. We were all thinking that. Everybody was thinking out there in the mud in the trenches. We were all thinking that. And also this was a chance, I was pretty raw, very raw as a musician. I had only been in the local, I joined in ’37 so I’d been in the local five years, and my experience — I was kind of limited. I had done little dance jobs playing with small groups. But we’ll probably get around to that as we go through my musical history. So I jumped at the chance. And it was a Godsend because in that band you had a lot of real stalwarts and real artists. You had Marshall Royal was our musical director. Marshall ended up being the lead alto player for Count Basie, and then when he left Count Basie he did studio work in Los Angeles and he was one of the most sought after
